title: Deploying a model: container, endpoint, autoscale, monitor
story:
Putting a model behind an endpoint makes it a service, and almost everything you already know about running a service applies unchanged. Health checks, versioned deploys, timeouts, the ability to roll back, alerting that wakes someone up. Start from there rather than from anything model-specific, because most of what goes wrong is ordinary and gets missed while attention is on the interesting parts.

Three things are genuinely different, and they are all consequences of the same fact: the weights are large.

Start time is the first. Loading a model is not a process starting in milliseconds; a container has to pull an image that contains a great deal of data, put the weights into memory, and only then serve anything. That breaks the assumption underneath most autoscaling, which is that new capacity arrives quickly when demand rises. Under a real spike, scaling that begins when the queue grows will finish long after the queue stopped mattering. So keep warm capacity you are willing to pay for while idle, bake the weights into the image rather than fetching them at start, and scale on a signal that leads demand rather than one that follows it.

Memory is the second, and it is usually the binding constraint rather than processor time. The weights occupy memory for the entire life of the process, and each concurrent request adds its own working memory on top, which grows with how much text is being processed. That gives you a concurrency limit that is a property of the hardware rather than a preference, and it should be enforced explicitly — a queue with a bounded length and a clear rejection is a system under load, while unbounded acceptance until memory runs out is a system that falls over and takes the in-flight requests with it.

The third is that throughput comes from grouping concurrent requests together, and that setting trades latency for capacity. A wider grouping serves more requests per unit of hardware and makes each individual one wait a little longer. Tune it against the target you set on the tail rather than by reasoning about what sounds efficient.

Treat the model version as a dependency, because it is exactly that. Deploy a new one alongside the old, send it real traffic or a replay of real traffic, compare on your case set, and keep the ability to route back to the previous version quickly. Anything that changes the output belongs in this — the weights, the decoding settings, the prompt that ships with them, the tokeniser. A change with no route back is not a deployment, it is a commitment.

Monitor what the service is doing, not only that it is alive. Queue depth and rejection rate tell you whether you are keeping up, memory headroom tells you how close the process is to dying, and the non-error indicators from the observability lesson tell you whether the answers changed. A model server that is healthy, responsive and producing worse answers than last week will pass every check in the first category.

And the honest part, which belongs in this lesson rather than a footnote: most teams should not be doing this. Hosted inference is somebody else's operational problem, priced per use, with no idle cost and no pager. The reasons to run it yourself are real but specific — data that legally cannot leave, volume steady and large enough that owning hardware is genuinely cheaper, latency you cannot achieve over somebody else's network, or a guarantee you need that no vendor will give you. What is not a reason is the per-token price looked at in isolation, because the comparison is not the token price against zero. It is the token price against hardware, plus the people who keep it running, plus the nights they are awake.

problem.practice: Time a cold start of your own serving setup, from nothing running to the first answer returned. Then look at your autoscaling rule and work out how long a spike would have to last for that new capacity to be useful. If the answer is longer than your spikes, your scaling policy is decoration and warm capacity is the actual mechanism.

beats.broke: Serving assumes processes start quickly and capacity is elastic, while loading weights is slow and memory is occupied for the life of the process.
beats.fix: Keep warm capacity with weights baked in, enforce an explicit bounded concurrency limit, tune grouping against the tail target, and deploy every version beside the last with a fast route back.
beats.cost: Warm capacity is paid for while idle, and the whole arrangement needs people — which is why hosted inference is the default unless a specific constraint says otherwise.

interview.q: What is genuinely different about serving a model, and when is self-hosting the right call?
interview.trap: Justifying self-hosting on the per-token price. The comparison is not against zero but against hardware plus the people who keep it running and the nights they are awake.
interview.answer:
Most of it is an ordinary service and should be run like one. What is different follows from the weights being large.

Start time: a container pulls a large image and loads weights before serving, which breaks the assumption that capacity arrives quickly. Scaling that begins when the queue grows finishes after the spike, so I keep warm capacity, bake the weights into the image, and scale on a leading signal.

Memory: the weights are resident for the life of the process and every concurrent request adds working memory, so the concurrency limit is a property of the hardware. I enforce it explicitly — a bounded queue with a clear rejection is a system under load, whereas accepting until memory runs out loses everything in flight.

Throughput comes from grouping concurrent requests, which trades latency for capacity, so it gets tuned against the tail target.

The model version is a dependency: deploy beside the old, compare on the case set with real or replayed traffic, keep a fast route back, and count everything that changes the output — weights, decoding settings, shipped prompt, tokeniser.

And I would monitor what it is doing rather than only that it is alive, because a server that is healthy, responsive and producing worse answers than last week passes every liveness check.

On self-hosting: usually not. The good reasons are data that cannot leave, steady volume large enough that hardware is genuinely cheaper, latency unachievable over someone else's network, or a guarantee no vendor gives. The per-token price alone is not one.
